We study appropriate reliance close to the actual decision that users have to make on the ground: whether or not to rely on a model output. We study this question in the context of physicians deciding when to rely on Machine Translation (MT) in an emergency room when communicating discharge instructions to a patient who does not speak their language.
datasets: University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) discharge instructions
De-identified Emergency Department discharge instructions (28 sentences)
de-identified Emergency Department (ED) discharge instructions that were written between the years 2016 to 2021 at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF)
outputs: Chinese translations of English discharge instruction sentences
automatically translated into simplified Chinese by Google Translate

Physicians were asked to read a discharge instruction, see the Chinese translation, and decide whether they would give the translation to a patient ... also assess whether a monolingual Chinese patient would understand the discharge instruction using a five‑point Likert scale.
Three bilingual physicians independently annotated each MT output along two dimensions: translation adequacy and clinical risk.
guideline: Annotators rated adequacy as accurate conveyance of meaning and clinical risk on categories: clinically insignificant, mildly clinically significant, moderately clinically significant, highly clinically significant, and life-threatening.

Annotators judged translation adequacy (whether the Chinese translation accurately conveyed the meaning) and clinical risk (five‑level categorization from clinically insignificant to life‑threatening). Physicians then answered binary decision questions and confidence/understandability Likert scales.

Adequacy was defined as whether the Chinese translation accurately conveyed the meaning of the English source text. Physicians rated clinical risk based on the translation presented to them according to five categories: clinically insignificant, mildly clinically significant, moderately clinically significant, highly clinically significant, and life-threatening.
